findings.evidence: Line 21 asserts the 60-day cutoff is "matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established," but the pilot section (lines 11 and 13, "What the Pilot Showed") reports only an aggregate 94%-vs-87% on-time-or-eventual return rate and a before/after fear-of-fines survey percentage (22% to 5%); it names no time-to-return distribution and no 60-day figure anywhere.
findings.fix: Either report the specific pilot figure that establishes a 60-day return-time pattern (e.g., what share of eventual returns arrived within 60 days vs. later), or remove the "matching...pilot data" justification and present the 60-day window as an operational choice made independently of the pilot findings.
findings.location: Recommendation section, third paragraph (line 21): "This recommendation applies to items returned within 60 days of their due date; items still unreturned past that window remain subject to the existing replacement-cost billing process, matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established."
findings.violation: A specific sub-claim (the 60-day billing cutoff matches an established pilot pattern) is presented as grounded in cited pilot data, but the artifact's own pilot description never reports the data point the claim invokes, so a reader cannot check this claim against anything the artifact supplies.

findings.evidence: Lines 29-33 raise and answer exactly one objection, the revenue/materials-funding concern ("A skeptic on the board points to overdue fines as a source of materials-replacement funding..."), answered with finance-record figures. Line 19 commits the systemwide rollout to a new notice mechanism, "replacing the current fine notices with automatic email reminders sent three, seven, and fourteen days after the due date," which the pilot description in lines 9-13 never mentions as part of what was tested, and the 16-month pilot itself (line 11) covered only 5 of the consortium's 10 branches.
findings.fix: Add a rebuttal passage addressing why the untested email-reminder mechanism should be expected to perform like whatever notice process the pilot branches actually used, and why the pilot's 5-branch results should be expected to hold at the other 5 branches, rather than leaving both open.
findings.location: "Addressing the Revenue Concern" section (lines 29-33), read against the Recommendation's description of the new notice mechanism (line 19) and the pilot description (lines 9-13).
findings.violation: The argument's own grounds leave open two foreseeable conditions it never raises or answers: whether a notice mechanism the pilot never describes testing will reproduce the pilot's return-rate and avoidance results, and whether results measured at 5 of 10 branches generalize to the other 5. Only the revenue objection is named and addressed; these are left unaddressed entirely.
